title: Goodwill After an Acquisition: The Private Company Elections
summary: Private company goodwill amortization under ASC 350-20: the ten-year election, the triggering event alternative, and when you still test for impairment.
body_markdown:
## Goodwill on the Consolidated Balance Sheet After Day One


Private company goodwill amortization is an election under ASC 350-20, not a default setting, and it lands on your desk the day after close. The purchase price allocation is signed, the measurement period is open, and a residual now sits on the consolidated balance sheet for the next decade. In most groups nobody formally decides what to do with it. Whoever closes the books that month picks a treatment, and that becomes policy. Indinero’s CPA-led team treats it as what it is, an accounting policy election with covenant, audit, and exit consequences.


Goodwill is the arithmetic remainder once every identifiable asset acquired and liability assumed is recognized at acquisition-date fair value. Our guide to[post-acquisition accounting integration](https://www.indinero.com/blog/post-acquisition-accounting-integration/) owns that derivation and the measurement period. This page picks up the day after. For the plain definition, see[what goodwill is](https://www.indinero.com/faq/what-is-goodwill/) .


### Why goodwill sits only in consolidation


Goodwill recognized in a business combination exists only on the acquirer’s consolidated balance sheet. The acquired entity’s standalone books keep historical carrying amounts. No goodwill line on the subsidiary’s trial balance, no intercompany entry that pushes it down, no eliminating entry that creates it. It gets built in the consolidation worksheet as a purchase accounting adjustment.


One exception matters.[ASU 2014-17](https://storage.fasb.org/ASU%202014-17.pdf) , in the pushdown accounting subsections of ASC 805-50, lets the acquired entity elect pushdown accounting in its own separate statements for the period of the change-in-control event. Elect it and the acquiree carries the goodwill on the acquirer’s new basis. Decline it and the standalone statements stay on historical basis. It matters the moment subsidiary statements go to a lender or a minority shareholder.


### The unit of account is the acquisition


Goodwill is tracked by acquisition, never as one pooled balance. Each amortizable unit corresponds to a distinct business combination, and a useful life is assigned acquisition by acquisition.


Amortizable unit Gross goodwill Useful life Accumulated amortization Net carrying amount


Existing at adoption $1,200,000 10 years $360,000 $840,000


Acquisition A (year 2) $3,400,000 10 years $680,000 $2,720,000


Acquisition B (year 3) $900,000 5 years $180,000 $720,000


Total $5,500,000 $1,220,000 $4,280,000


Year-three amortization there is $640,000, debited to amortization expense against accumulated amortization of goodwill. Public business entities, by contrast, still carry goodwill as indefinite-lived and test it annually under ASC 350-20-35-28. FASB put the subsequent accounting for goodwill on its technical agenda in 2018, leaned toward amortization with a ten-year default, then voted unanimously on June 15, 2022 to drop the project.


Amortization isn’t coming to public GAAP.


## The Private Company Amortization Alternative


A private company may elect to amortize goodwill straight line over ten years, or less if a shorter life is demonstrable. This is the goodwill accounting alternative ASC 350-20 provides, a Private Company Council consensus issued as ASU 2014-02, with the requirement at ASC 350-20-35-63. Electing it makes goodwill a finite-lived asset and replaces annual impairment testing with trigger-only testing.


**Who can elect it.** Entities that aren’t public business entities under the ASC Master Glossary.[ASU 2019-06](https://storage.fasb.org/ASU%202019-06.pdf) extended this alternative, and the companion ASU 2014-18 intangibles alternative, to not-for-profit entities.


**What “irrevocable” actually means.** ASU 2016-03 removed the effective dates for the Private Company Council alternatives, so a private company can adopt in any future period without a preferability assessment under ASC 250. Changing back is the hard part. A later change has to be justified as preferable, and your auditor has to accept the conclusion. Going in is free. Coming out isn’t.


**Ten years, or shorter if you can defend it.** Amortizing goodwill over ten years is the default, and the default needs no justification. A shorter life is permitted where the entity demonstrates another useful life is more appropriate, which takes documented support, usually the remaining contractual term of the revenue contracts that drove the price. ASC 350-20-35-64 allows a later revision as a change in estimate, but the cumulative period for any amortizable unit can’t exceed ten years. You can shorten. You can’t extend.


**The level election at ASC 350-20-35-65.** On adoption the entity also elects, as policy, to test at the entity level or the reporting unit level. Entity level means no reporting units have to be identified at all, which for a $1M to $20M group running one operating business is real work removed. Groups with several legal entities still need the[multi-entity accounting](https://www.indinero.com/blog/multi-entity-accounting-guide/) discipline underneath, since amortization is tracked by unit either way.


**The ASU 2014-18 companion.** ASU 2014-18 skips separate recognition of customer-related intangibles unless they’re capable of being sold or licensed independently, and subsumes all acquired noncompetition agreements into goodwill. Mortgage servicing rights and customer information databases still get recognized separately. Ordinary customer relationships don’t. The dependency runs one way. Elect ASU 2014-18 and you must also adopt ASU 2014-02, but not the reverse.


On an $8,000,000 deal that moves $1,800,000 of customer relationships and $250,000 of noncompetes into the residual, taking goodwill from $2,950,000 to $5,000,000. Total amortization expense isn’t obviously lower. It’s just far less to compute, support, and audit.


## The Triggering Event Alternative


The goodwill triggering event alternative lets a private company or not-for-profit evaluate triggering events only as of the end of each reporting period. It came from[ASU 2021-03](https://storage.fasb.org/ASU%202021-03.pdf) , it’s codified at ASC 350-20-35-83 through 35-86, and the scope paragraph is ASC 350-20-15-4A. An electing entity isn’t required to monitor for triggering events during the period at all.


ASC 350-20-35-84 is the operative permission. The evaluation happens “only as of the end of each reporting period, whether the reporting period is an interim or annual period.” ASC 350-20-35-85 limits the alternative to goodwill, leaving the requirements for other assets untouched. ASC 350-20-35-86 prohibits retroactive application to interim periods for which annual statements have already been issued.


One citation note, because this block gets mixed up constantly. ASC 350-20-35-83 through 35-86 is the triggering event alternative, not the impairment test. That model is ASC 350-20-35-65 through 35-82.


**The two elections are independent.** ASC 350-20-15-6 says it outright: “An entity that elects either of the accounting alternatives in this Subtopic is not required to elect or precluded from electing the other alternative.” Four valid positions. Amortization only. Triggering event only. Both. Neither. Most growth-stage groups assume it’s one election, which is how they end up with half a policy.


**Who it helps, and who it doesn’t.** The relief is largest for entities that issue only annual statements, because what’s removed is the obligation to catch an impairment that existed mid-period and then recovered.[Journal of Accountancy’s reporting](https://www.journalofaccountancy.com/issues/2022/jun/goodwill-triggering-event-alternative-provides-relief-some-companies/) quotes a practitioner plainly: “For private companies issuing quarterly GAAP financial statements, this alternative is not going to help them too much.” One downside. An entity that later becomes ineligible has to reverse the effects, which can mean rebuilding retrospective interim assessments without using hindsight.


**What a triggering event looks like for a $1M to $20M group.** ASC 350-20-35-3C gives seven categories, (a) through (g), and the list isn’t all-inclusive. Category (g), share price, has no private analogue, so (d) overall financial performance and (e) entity-specific events do the work. In practice that’s the loss of a major customer who sat in the cash flow forecast behind the price, the departure of the acquired founder, a down round, sustained losses behind the allocation model, or a covenant breach. Put the evaluation in writing on the reporting-date close checklist, with the evidence discipline our[audit prep checklist](https://www.indinero.com/blog/audit-prep-for-startups-checklist/) applies everywhere else.


## Testing Goodwill for Impairment


Goodwill impairment testing for private companies that elected amortization happens only on a triggering event, never on a calendar. The model is ASC 350-20-35-65 through 35-82, added by ASU 2014-02. One step, at the level elected on adoption, with the loss capped at the carrying amount of goodwill.


1. **Did a triggering event occur.** ASC 350-20-35-66 requires testing only “if an event occurs or circumstances change that indicate that the fair value of the entity (or the reporting unit) may be below its carrying amount.” With the ASU 2021-03 election, that question is asked as of the reporting date.
2. **Optional qualitative assessment.** ASC 350-20-35-67 and the paragraphs following permit a qualitative test of whether it’s more likely than not that fair value is less than carrying amount. Answer no and testing stops there.
3. **The one-step quantitative test.** ASC 350-20-35-73 measures the loss as the amount by which carrying amount including goodwill exceeds fair value, “limited to the total amount of goodwill.” That cap does real work. Nothing but goodwill gets written down, and the loss stays bounded.
4. **Allocate across amortizable units.** ASC 350-20-35-77 allocates the loss “on a pro rata basis using their relative carrying amounts or using another reasonable and rational basis.” This is the paragraph that makes the subledger mandatory.
5. **Reset the basis.** ASC 350-20-35-78 makes the adjusted carrying amount the new accounting basis, amortized over each unit’s remaining useful life. Reversal is prohibited. If the business recovers, the goodwill does not come back.


Ordering matters. Under ASC 350-20-35-79 and 35-80 the other assets are tested before goodwill, because a long-lived asset write-down changes the carrying amount feeding the goodwill test. That amount comes off the consolidation, so the[multi-entity consolidation process](https://www.indinero.com/blog/multi-entity-consolidation-process/) has to be reconciled before the test means anything.


Worked through the subledger above: entity-level testing elected, net goodwill $4,280,000, total carrying amount $9,200,000, fair value determined at $7,500,000. The excess is $1,700,000, below the cap, so the full amount is recognized and allocated pro rata. That’s $333,700 to the adoption-date unit, $1,080,400 to Acquisition A, and $285,900 to Acquisition B. Had fair value instead been $4,500,000, the excess of $4,700,000 would exceed total goodwill, the loss would stop at $4,280,000, and the remaining $420,000 of shortfall would go unrecognized.


## Common Pitfalls


Each failure below is paired with the subsection that makes it one.


1. **Electing amortization without reading the credit agreement.** The election doesn’t change EBITDA, because amortization is added back. It does change net income, operating income, net assets, and retained earnings. A covenant keyed to net income, a fixed charge coverage ratio, or a tangible net worth test can tighten the moment the first entry posts. Read the defined terms for Consolidated Net Income and Consolidated EBITDA before the election, not at the next compliance certificate.
2. **No contemporaneous documentation.** Adoption needs no preferability assessment, but it does need a policy memo: the ASU 2014-02 election, the ASU 2014-18 decision, the level election, the useful life assigned at adoption and the basis for anything under ten years, and the ASU 2021-03 election. Memory is not an audit position.
3. **Ten years by default when the acquired contracts run five.** Ten years needs no justification, which makes it the path of least resistance. If the deal was priced off a contract portfolio with a five-year weighted average term, a ten-year life overstates carrying amount in years six through ten, exactly when a triggering event is most likely.
4. **Never revisiting triggering events.** Trigger-only testing becomes never testing without a deliberate process. Make it a standing close-checklist item, documented, walked against the seven categories at ASC 350-20-35-3C. Groups that skipped ASU 2021-03 owe continuous monitoring instead, which is heavier and is itself an argument for the election.
5. **One blended goodwill balance.** Mechanically fatal, three ways. ASC 350-20-35-63 requires amortization of goodwill relating to each business combination. The cumulative cap at ASC 350-20-35-64 is per unit. And ASC 350-20-35-77 requires allocating any loss across units, so a blended balance can’t isolate the impairment to the acquisition that failed.
6. **Confusing the GAAP election with the tax deduction.** Acquired goodwill is a section 197 intangible, and the[IRS rule](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/intangibles) is 15-year amortization of the capitalized costs of section 197 intangibles acquired after August 10, 1993, subject to the anti-churning rules. That period has nothing to do with the GAAP useful life, and the deduction doesn’t depend on the election at all. Indinero’s[business tax services](https://www.indinero.com/services/business-tax-services/) team owns that reconciliation.
7. **Electing while an exit is on the roadmap.** An IPO, or an acquisition by a public filer, unwinds the alternatives retrospectively. Historical statements for all periods presented must comply with public company GAAP: reverse prior amortization, re-perform purchase price allocations to measure the intangibles ASU 2014-18 subsumed, re-perform impairment testing at the reporting unit level. On a realistic two to three year exit horizon the alternatives are often a false economy, a judgment that belongs in your[exit planning and valuation](https://www.indinero.com/blog/exit-planning-the-art-and-science-of-valuations/) thinking. For a long-hold private group with bank debt and no public path, they’re usually worth electing.

## Frequently asked questions


These are the questions that come up most once a group has closed its first deal and the goodwill is sitting on the consolidated balance sheet. Short answers below, with the governing subsection named wherever the answer turns on it.


### Does a private company have to test goodwill for impairment every year?


A private company that elected goodwill amortization under ASC 350-20 has no annual impairment test and evaluates goodwill only when a triggering event occurs. Annual testing applies to public business entities under ASC 350-20-35-28 and to private companies that didn’t make the election. If you elected amortization, the discipline shifts from a calendar date to a documented evaluation against the seven triggering event categories at ASC 350-20-35-3C, ideally a standing item on the close checklist.


### Can a company that amortizes goodwill still record an impairment?


A company that amortizes goodwill still records impairment when a triggering event occurs, with the loss limited to the carrying amount of goodwill. The model sits at ASC 350-20-35-65 through 35-82, tested at the entity or reporting unit level elected on adoption. ASC 350-20-35-73 caps the loss at total goodwill, and ASC 350-20-35-77 allocates it pro rata across amortizable units. The adjusted carrying amount becomes the new basis, and reversal is prohibited.


### Do lenders or investors object to amortized goodwill?


Lenders rarely object to goodwill amortization because it’s added back to EBITDA, but covenants keyed to net income or tangible net worth can tighten. Read the defined terms for Consolidated Net Income and Consolidated EBITDA before electing, which is the kind of modeling indinero’s CFO advisory does alongside the close. Equity investors raise the sharper objection, since anyone expecting an IPO or a sale to a public filer knows the alternatives have to be unwound retrospectively.


### What happens to the election if the company later goes public?


An IPO or an acquisition by a public filer unwinds the private company goodwill alternatives retrospectively for every period presented. That means reversing prior amortization, re-performing the purchase price allocations to measure the intangibles ASU 2014-18 subsumed into goodwill, and re-performing impairment testing at the reporting unit level. On a realistic two to three year exit horizon the alternatives often cost more to unwind than they ever saved, which is why the decision belongs in exit planning, not in the close.


### Over what period should goodwill be amortized if not ten years?


Goodwill can be amortized over fewer than ten years when the entity demonstrates a shorter useful life is more appropriate, never over more. ASC 350-20-35-63 sets ten years as the default and it needs no justification, while a shorter life needs documented support, usually the remaining contractual term of the revenue contracts that drove the purchase price. ASC 350-20-35-64 permits a later revision as a change in estimate, but cumulative amortization for any unit can’t exceed ten years.


### Is amortized goodwill deductible on the tax return?


GAAP goodwill amortization isn’t itself a tax deduction, because acquired goodwill is deducted as a section 197 intangible over 15 years instead. The two regimes run independently, so the 15-year period applies to section 197 intangibles acquired after August 10, 1993 whether or not you elected the GAAP alternative, and the difference between the schedules is permanent. Indinero’s bundled engagement keeps the useful life decision and the return claiming that deduction in the same hands.


### How is goodwill tracked when a group has acquired several entities?


Goodwill is tracked by acquisition as separate amortizable units, never as one blended balance, with a useful life assigned deal by deal. ASC 350-20-35-63 requires amortization of goodwill relating to each business combination, and ASC 350-20-35-77 requires any impairment loss to be allocated pro rata across those units, which a pooled balance can’t support. Note that the testing level elected under ASC 350-20-35-65, entity or reporting unit, is a separate question from the tracking unit, and a subledger by amortizable unit handles both.
